nameStory: Seaside Threeawn gets its name from its coastal habitat and its distinctive seed heads, each topped with three long, needle-like projections called awns. These three-pronged awns look like tiny pitchforks and help the seeds catch the wind and find new places to grow in the sandy dunes.
description: Seaside Threeawn is a slender annual grass that thrives in New England's coastal areas. This wispy grass typically grows 1-2 feet tall with narrow leaves and delicate, open seed heads that dance in ocean breezes. It's perfectly adapted to sandy, salty conditions where few other plants can survive, forming small clumps that help stabilize dune systems.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Each seed bears three thin, wire-like awns that spread apart like a tiny trident - this three-pronged feature is the plant's signature characteristic and feels rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, wispy clumps with multiple thin stems that sway gracefully in coastal winds, creating an airy, delicate appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, thread-like leaves that feel somewhat stiff and rough when rubbed between fingers, often curling inward during dry conditions

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, wiry stems that feel firm but flexible, often with a slight reddish tinge near the base

idTips.label: Overall Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant has a dry, papery feel when mature, rustling softly in the breeze with a subtle scratchy sound

habitat: Look for Seaside Threeawn in sandy coastal areas including dunes, beaches, and salt marshes along New England's Atlantic shoreline. It thrives in loose, well-draining sandy soils that can tolerate salt spray and harsh coastal conditions. You'll often find it growing alongside beach pea, seaside goldenrod, and other salt-tolerant coastal plants.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge as small tufts of narrow green leaves, easily overlooked among other emerging beach vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and develop their characteristic open, branching seed heads with the distinctive three-awned seeds.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads turn golden-brown and become more prominent as seeds mature and disperse, creating the plant's most recognizable appearance.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through winter, appearing as bleached, papery skeletons that eventually break apart in storms.

funFact: The three needle-like awns on each seed can actually drill themselves into the sand by twisting and untwisting with changes in humidity, literally screwing the seed into the ground for better germination - nature's own self-planting mechanism!
confusionNotes: Other threeawn grasses share the three-awned seed feature, but Seaside Threeawn is the only one you'll find growing directly in coastal sand dunes and beaches. If you're not within sight and smell of the ocean, you're probably looking at a different threeawn species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'seaside needlegrass,' this plant isn't related to true needlegrasses and the 'needles' refer to the sharp awns, not the leaves. The scientific name 'tuberculosa' refers to small bumps or tubercles found on parts of the plant.
compareHints: Seaside Threeawn is distinguished from other New England threeawns primarily by its coastal habitat - it's the only species in the genus that grows directly in beach sand and tolerates salt spray. While Arrowfeather Threeawn and others may have similar three-awned seeds, they prefer inland dry fields and prairies rather than oceanfront locations.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the three-awn grasses in New England, Slim-spike has the most delicate, narrow flower spikes - much thinner than the more robust spikes of Arrowfeather Threeawn or the branched clusters of Fork-tip Three-awn.

Arrowfeather threeawn is typically taller and more robust than most of its relatives like fork-tip three-awn, and its seed bristles are usually longer and more feathery than the shorter, stiffer bristles of oldfield three-awn.
Among its three-awn relatives in New England, Oldfield Three-awn is the most delicate and branched, with the most open, airy seed heads.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, fork-tip three-awn is unique for its distinctly forked branching pattern and smaller size.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, forked three-awn is distinguished by its branching pattern from the base rather than higher up the stem like fork-tip three-awn.
